issues.legal_issue: Public interest must be considered both when approving a cinema site and when licensing the exhibition of films, using factors relevant to each stage, without reopening final determinations made at the site-approval stage.
material_facts: The site was approved after the licensing authority determined that the nearby organisation was not a qualifying educational or residential institution for the applicable location restriction.
The authority later considered an application to license the completed cinema and relied on objections concerning the organisation’s proximity and the effects of a cinema on the locality.
issues.conclusion: Public interest is relevant at both stages, but its parameters may differ; matters finally determined during site approval cannot be reconsidered under the guise of public interest when deciding the later licence application.
issues.legal_principle: Under Rule 3 and Rules 4 and 7 of the U.P. Cinematograph Rules, 1951, public interest may be considered when approving a site, and Rule 7(2)(c) requires sufficient written reasons and prior State Government approval for refusal on that ground. Under sections 3 and 5(1)(c) of the U.P. Cinema (Regulation) Act, 1955, public interest must also be considered when deciding whether to grant an exhibition licence, but the relevant factors at that stage may differ. The explanation to Rule 7 makes the licensing authority’s determination of whether an institution qualifies final and conclusive. The court distinguished The King v. London County Council, Ex parte London and Provincial Electric Theatres Limited and R. v. Barnstaple Justices, Ex parte Carder because their statutory schemes differed.

predicates.cinema_exhibition_licence_application: A person applied to the licensing authority for permission to exhibit films in a cinema building.
predicates.prior_site_approval_resolved_location_is: The licensing authority approved the site after deciding a location-related issue that the governing process makes final.
predicates.later_licence_decision_revisits_that_iss: The licensing authority relied on that already-decided location-related issue when considering the exhibition licence.

issues.definition: When an exhibition-licence decision revisits a location issue finally resolved during site approval, the decision must use the factors relevant to the licence stage without reopening that determination.

issues.legal_issue: A licensing authority’s refusal of an exhibition licence on irrelevant or arbitrary grounds is subject to judicial interference.
material_facts: The licensing authority refused the licence on public-interest grounds that included objections about noise, traffic, and disturbance to the nearby organisation’s surroundings.

The cinema was sound-proof, and the location-related objections had already been dealt with during site approval; the court found the refusal reflected the organisation’s opposition rather than relevant public-interest considerations.
issues.conclusion: The refusal was based on extraneous and irrelevant considerations, so the refusal order was quashed and set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Licensing powers, although broad, must be exercised on relevant considerations germane to the decision and not oppressively or arbitrarily. A court may intervene where a licence is refused on irrelevant grounds. Sections 3 and 5 of the U.P. Cinema (Regulation) Act, 1955 govern the exhibition licence and require satisfaction that granting it is not contrary to public interest.

predicates.cinema_exhibition_licence_application: A person applied to the licensing authority for permission to exhibit films in a cinema building.
predicates.licence_refusal_rests_on_irrelevant_cons: The licensing authority refused the application based on considerations unrelated to the lawful decision it had to make.

issues.definition: If an exhibition-licence refusal rests on irrelevant considerations, the refusal is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A court exercising writ jurisdiction cannot direct a statutory licensing authority to grant a licence before that authority has performed its statutory decision-making function.
material_facts: The challenged order remitted the licence application to the licensing authority for reconsideration.
The High Court directed the authority to grant the licence even though the authority had not yet completed its statutory consideration of the application.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could quash the remand order if it was legally erroneous, but it could not take over the licensing authority’s function and direct it to grant the licence; the mandamus was set aside to that extent.
issues.legal_principle: Where a statute confers a power and requires an authority to perform a function before exercising that power, a court in writ jurisdiction cannot supplant the authority and perform that function itself.

predicates.writ_proceeding_challenges_remand: A person brought a writ proceeding challenging an order that sent a licensing matter back for reconsideration.
predicates.statutory_authority_has_not_decided_lice: The statutory licensing authority had not yet completed its consideration of the licence application.

issues.definition: When a writ proceeding challenges a remand while the statutory authority has not decided the licence application, the court cannot direct that authority to grant the licence before it decides.
